system:
You audit the knowledge atoms of one Knowledge Card. A card is the answer key for a benchmark of expert conceptual knowledge, so every atom must be correct, self-contained, and assessable on its own.

Judge every atom on every check listed below. Rules:
- For checks about evidence, use only the evidence sentences supplied with the atom. Do not repair an atom with your own knowledge.
- For GROUNDED, use "hold" when unreadable PDF symbols prevent verification; explain what is needed. Use fail only when the available evidence is sufficient to determine that the claim is unsupported. This hold rule takes precedence over the strictness rule. Judge other checks independently using their listed values; do not invent missing facts.
- Be strict within each check's allowed values. Do not turn an inability to verify GROUNDED into revise or fail; use hold as defined above.
- "why" is required for every value other than the first listed value; keep it under 30 words. Omit "why" when passing.

Checks (allowed values in brackets; the first value means no problem):
- GROUNDED [pass / revise / fail / hold]: The cited evidence sentences state the atom, including its specificity, causal force, assumptions, and certainty. pass = fully stated. revise = partly stated (the atom adds, drops, or strengthens something; say what). fail = not stated when the available evidence permits a judgment. hold = unreadable symbols prevent verification. For pass or revise, put the supporting evidence ids in cite.
- SINGLE_CLAIM [pass / revise]: The atom is one independently assessable claim. revise = it joins two or more claims that could be true or false separately. Evidence spanning more than three sentences is not by itself a reason to split or revise an atom.
- SCOPE_LABEL [pass / revise]: The S label fits (S1 what it is / S2 how it works / S3 where it ends). revise = wrong label; put the right one in why, e.g. 'S2: ...'.
- L1_ONLY [pass / fail]: The atom is recall-level knowledge. fail = knowing it requires applying the concept to a new problem, or combining facts from distant passages.
- SOURCE_INDEPENDENT [pass / revise / fail]: A domain expert who never read this book could judge the claim true or false. revise = phrased as the authors' statement but the claim itself is general (drop the attribution). fail = an isolated study finding, conjecture, or author-specific opinion, classification, or recommendation, even if attribution was removed. Explicitly scoped established facts about a formalism or architecture and conditional theoretical results remain eligible.
- NO_OVERLAP [pass / fail]: No other atom in this card states or contains the same claim. If two atoms overlap, fail only the less informative one and put the other atom's id in cite; the other one passes.
- CENTRALITY [pass / fail]: The atom matters for understanding the concept. fail = peripheral detail.
Whole-card checks (report under "batch"):
- CONCEPT_SCOPE [pass / fail]: The concept is a general concept of the field. fail = a topic whose assessable content is restricted to excluded study-specific findings or author-specific positions. A named formalism, system, or architecture is not disqualified solely for being specific if its scoped conceptual facts are source-independent.

Output ONLY one JSON object:
{"units": {"<atom_id>": {"<CHECK>": {"v": "<value>", "why": "", "cite": []}, ...}, ...}, "batch": {"<CHECK>": {"v": "<value>", "why": ""}}}

CONCEPT: Probabilistic relational Hoare logic
ASSESSMENT SCOPE: pRHL as a logic for coupling proofs: judgments relating two programs, the lifting-based interpretation of pre- and postconditions, the two-sided, one-sided and structural rules (Sample with a bijection, While, Seq, Case, Equiv), the losslessness side condition for one-sided loop rules, and what valid judgments imply. Excludes approximate and quantitative extensions.

ATOMS:
- CS-PL-C04-S1-01 | S1
  ATOM: The proof rules of pRHL represent different ways to combine liftings, formalizing various steps in coupling proofs, so pRHL can be interpreted as a formal logic for proofs by coupling.
  EVIDENCE:
    [CS-PL-p0174-s11] More importantly, the proof rules represent different ways to combine liftings, formalizing various steps in coupling proofs.
    [CS-PL-p0174-s12] Accordingly, we will interpret pRHL as a formal logic for proofs by coupling.
- CS-PL-C04-S1-02 | S1
  ATOM: A pRHL judgment encodes a probabilistic relational property of two programs, where the post-condition describes a probabilistic lifting between the two output distributions.
  EVIDENCE:
    [CS-PL-p0174-s10] Judgments encode probabilistic relational properties of two programs, where a post-condition describes a probabilistic liftings between two output distributions.
- CS-PL-C04-S1-03 | S1
  ATOM: Compared to standard program logics, probabilistic Relational Hoare Logic (pRHL) differs in two ways: each judgment describes two programs, and the programs can use random sampling.
  EVIDENCE:
    [CS-PL-p0174-s08] Compared to standard program logics, there are two twists: each judgment describes two programs,1 and programs can use random sampling.
- CS-PL-C04-S2-01 | S2

  EVIDENCE:
    [CS-PL-p0185-s06] In more detail, a valid judgment ρ |= c1 ∼c2 : Φ =⇒Ψ implies that for any two input memories related by Φ, there exists a coupling with support in Ψ between the two output distributions.
- CS-PL-C04-S2-02 | S2

    [CS-PL-p0180-s19] In some ways it is the key rule in pRHL, allowing us to select a coupling for a pair of sampling instructions.
- CS-PL-C04-S2-03 | S2

- CS-PL-C04-S3-01 | S3
  ATOM: The one-sided pRHL loop rules require the side-condition that the loop is lossless (it produces a proper distribution with total probability 1) because skip produces a proper distribution on any input and liftings can only relate sub-distributions with equal weights, so the loop must also produce a proper distribution to have any hope of coupling the output distributions.
  EVIDENCE:
    [CS-PL-p0183-s10] Losslessness is needed for soundness: skip produces a proper distribution on any input and liftings can only relate sub-distributions with equal weights (Theorem 5.9), so the loop must also produce a proper distribution to have any hope of coupling the output distributions.
- CS-PL-C04-S3-02.r1 | S3
  ATOM: The two-sided pRHL rules in Fig. 5.2 apply when the two programs in the conclusion judgment have the same top-level shape.
  EVIDENCE:
    [CS-PL-p0180-s14] The two-sided rules in Fig. 5.2 apply when the two programs in the conclusion judgment have the same top-level shape.
- CS-PL-C04-S3-03 | S3
  ATOM: The two-sided pRHL loop rule can only analyze two loops in a synchronized fashion, so it cannot relate two loops that run for different numbers of iterations (for example when $T_1 < T_2$), no matter how the samples are coupled.
  EVIDENCE:
    [CS-PL-p0188-s10] The main obstacle is that the two-sided loop rule in pRHL can only analyze loops in a synchronized fashion, but this is not possible here: when T1 < T2 the two loops run for different numbers of iterations, no matter how we couple the samples.
- CS-PL-C04-S3-04 | S3
  ATOM: The soundness of the special-case sampling rule that couples a distribution $d$ with itself through a bijection $f : \mathrm{supp}(d) \to \mathrm{supp}(d)$ crucially relies on $d$ being uniform.
  EVIDENCE:

    [CS-PL-p0181-s03] It is possible to support more general distributions at the cost of a more complicated side-condition,2 but we will not need this generality.
